title: Resurfaced Road Stretches
story: Several crews resurfaced a country road this summer. Each logged its stretch as a pair of kilometre markers, like [3, 6] for kilometres 3 to 6. Crews often overlapped, and the log is in no particular order.
The county wants a clean map for drivers: the fewest stretches that show exactly which parts of the road are new.
task: Write mergeStretches(jobs). Each job is [start, end] with start ≤ end. Return the combined stretches as [start, end] pairs, sorted by start, with no two overlapping or touching.
Two jobs belong to the same stretch if they share any point, even just an endpoint: [2, 5] and [5, 9] become [2, 9]. An empty log returns an empty list.

examples.explanation: Sorted by start: [1, 4], [3, 6], [8, 10]. The first two share kilometres 3 to 4, so together they cover 1 to 6. The job at 8 starts after 6, leaving a gap of old road.
One crew stopped at kilometre 5 and another started at 5, so there is no gap: 2 to 9 is one continuous new stretch.

hints: In the first example as logged, [8, 10] comes first but is the last stretch on the road. What would make it easier to see which jobs touch?
Sort the jobs by start. Now, can a job overlap a stretch you finished long ago, or only the most recent one?
After sorting, keep a current stretch. The next job either starts at or before its end (and joins it) or starts after it (and begins a new stretch).

Sort by start. Put the first job in the result. For each next job: if its start ≤ the end of the last stretch, set that end to the larger of the two ends. Otherwise append the job. Mind the "larger of the two ends": a short job inside a long one must not shrink it.
bruteForce: Scan all pairs of stretches; whenever two overlap, replace them with their union and start over. Stop when no pair overlaps, then sort.
Each scan checks O(n²) pairs, and you may need up to n scans: O(n³), around a trillion comparisons for 10,000 jobs. The waste is checking pairs that are far apart on the road.

tests.note: end must be max, not last

js: last[1] = Math.max(last[1], end); // joins the current stretch
result.push([start, end]); // gap before it: new stretch
py: result[-1][1] = max(result[-1][1], end)  # joins the current stretch
result.append([start, end])  # gap before it: new stretch
walkthrough: Once sorted by start, a job can only overlap the stretch you are building now. Every earlier stretch ended before the current one began, and this job starts even later. So one pass is enough.
• [1, 4]: the result is empty, so start a stretch. Result: [[1, 4]].
• [3, 6]: 3 ≤ 4, so it joins. The end becomes max(4, 6) = 6. Result: [[1, 6]].
Two details trip people up. Use ≤, not <, because touching stretches join. And take the max of the ends: in [1, 10], [2, 3] the second job must not cut the stretch short.
solution.timeWhy: The sort dominates; the sweep is one pass.
solution.spaceWhy: The sorted copy and the result list.
solution.takeaway: Sort intervals by start, then sweep once, comparing each interval only with the last one kept. Most interval problems start with this sort-then-sweep step.
